human_tolerance.notes: 'In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders.' flight_distance_m and light_max are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

phases.name: flocking
phases.note: Northern birds 'migrate further south, arriving in their winter quarters between mid-September and November'; winter flocks may contain several different subspecies and are nicknamed a 'blizzard'.

phases.name: dispersal
phases.note: 'leaving to breed from mid-March onwards, with almost all of them gone by the end of April or so.' Many populations are permanent residents or altitudinal migrants instead - in the Sierra Nevada, eastern California, J. hyemalis winters 5,000-7,000 feet (1,500-2,100 m) below its summer range - and in cold years birds may stay on their winter range and breed there.

phases.name: breeding
phases.note: 'The dark-eyed junco's breeding habitat is coniferous or mixed forest areas throughout North America.' Nesting starts soon after the return; normally two clutches of four eggs. The slightly glossy eggs are grayish or pale bluish-white and heavily spotted with shades of brown, purple or gray, concentrated at the large end; the female incubates for 12 to 13 days and the young leave the nest between 11 and 14 days after hatching.

phases.name: nesting
phases.note: Nests are usually 'a cup-shaped depression on the ground, well-hidden by vegetation or other material, although nests are sometimes found in the lower branches of a shrub or tree', about 10 cm across and lined with fine grasses and hair.

vocalizations.description: 'The song is a trill similar to the chipping sparrow's, except that the red-backed dark-eyed junco's song is more complex, similar to that of the yellow-eyed junco.' Sung from a low perch or the ground in the breeding territories.

'The call also resembles that of the black-throated blue warbler... Calls include tick sounds and very high-pitched tinkling chips.' It fills the shared program's alarm slot, since the source describes no separate alarm call; loudness and cooldown are judgement.

external.note: GBIF usage key, authorship and order from the GBIF Backbone Taxonomy; the iNaturalist taxa API matched taxon 10094 to 'Dark-eyed Junco'; ITIS TSN and NCBI taxon id from Wikidata (P815, P685).

conservation.note: Wikidata P141 = least concern. The Wikipedia article carries no conservation section, so the CC0 Wikidata statement is the authority here.

range.note: 'It is common across much of temperate North America and in summer it ranges far into the Arctic', breeding in 'coniferous or mixed forest areas throughout North America', with wintering birds reaching the northeastern United States and a resident subspecies in the Carolinas; the slate-colored subspecies is a rare vagrant to western Europe. The state list is an approximation covering the contiguous United States plus Alaska and is not exhaustive. No elevation range is given for the species as a whole, so elevation_m is omitted (the Sierra Nevada altitudinal figure of 1,500-2,100 m applies to one population, not the species).

traits.note: Covers the structural traits (body plan, limb count, thermoregulation, skin, flight, respiration, metamorphosis, perching) and locomotion modes: 'These birds forage on the ground', the white outer tail feathers 'flash distinctively... while hopping on the ground', and the species is a short-distance flyer between winter grounds, breeding territories and feeders.

traits.nest_type.note: 'Dark-eyed juncos usually nest in a cup-shaped depression on the ground, well-hidden by vegetation or other material, although nests are sometimes found in the lower branches of a shrub or tree.'

traits.size_class.note: From mass_kg (~0.024 kg, an 18-30 g range); the validator's size-class bands place this in the Tiny band.

traits.mass_kg.note: Midpoint of the stated 18-30 g range, 24 g.

traits.wingspan_m.note: Midpoint of the stated 18-25 cm wingspan, as a direct conversion of the sourced value.

traits.lifespan_y.note: HONEST GAP: no lifespan figure for Junco hyemalis was found in any CC0 or CC BY source. Inferred from a close relative in the sense AGENTS.md allows: the song sparrow (Melospiza melodia), a New World sparrow of the same family Passerellidae - the junco article itself groups it with 'the related fox sparrow' of that family - has a 'maximum lifespan in the wild' of 11.3 years (Wikipedia). Half that record, 5.6 years, is the usual rough relationship between a record longevity and a typical one in a small passerine. This is an order-of-magnitude estimate, not a measured value for this species.

traits.diet.note: 'They mainly eat seeds and insects, with seeds comprising three quarters of their year-round diet. However, during the breeding season, insects comprise nearly half of the diet of adult dark-eyed juncos. Young dark-eyed juncos also depend on a diet of mainly insects.' The year-round split is used; the seasonal shift is recorded in seasonal.phases instead of being modelled as separate resource weights.

traits.social.note: Judgement: the source describes winter flocks and a single-brood territory system but not the pair bond; a Pair breeding unit is inferred from 'the female incubates' and from two clutches per season being the norm for a monogamous New World sparrow. Non-breeding birds flock, sometimes mixing subspecies.

traits.activity_pattern.note: Judgement: the source describes daytime ground foraging, morning song and the flock's 'blizzard' nickname, and does not label the pattern.

traits.defense.note: Judgement: no sourced predator defence; the shared perching-songbird program's default response to a close threat is to move away, so Flee was authored.

traits.wariness.note: Judgement: 'In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders' - a tame feeder bird, but one that flushes readily, so a low-middling value was authored.

habitat.note: Covers shelter_tag and habitat.resources. Seed and invertebrate tags come from Behavior and ecology; nest_ground from the ground cup nest; perch from low song perches and winter flocking in shrubs. Weights are judgement, not separately sourced percentages.

habitat.use.note: 'These birds forage on the ground'; the white outer tail feathers flash 'while hopping on the ground'; trees are used for nesting in low branches, for song perches and as winter cover.

habitat.human_tolerance.note: Distribution and habitat section: 'In winter, dark-eyed juncos are familiar in and around towns, and in many places are the most common birds at feeders.' flight_distance_m and light_max are judgement, not separately sourced numbers.

seasonal.strategy.note: 'Northern birds migrate further south... Many populations are permanent residents or altitudinal migrants, while in cold years they may choose to stay in their winter range and breed there' - a partial migrant with a resident and an altitudinal component, so PartialMigration was used.

seasonal.phases.note: Winter flocking from mid-September to November, the return to breed from mid-March with most gone by the end of April, breeding in coniferous or mixed forest with the quoted clutch, incubation and nestling figures, and the ground cup nest. Day-of-month boundaries come from the source's 'mid-September', 'mid-March' and 'end of April'; the breeding end date is judgement because the source gives no end. The breeding phase is tagged US-CO because the locale that prompted this record is in Colorado; the source's dates are continental.

seasonal.life_stages.note: Egg (grayish or pale bluish-white, heavily spotted, about four per clutch) and altricial juvenile ('juveniles often have pale streaks on their underparts and may even be mistaken for vesper sparrows until they acquire adult plumage at two to three months'; leaving the nest 11-14 days after hatching) and adult. No sourced period of juvenile plumage was found beyond the two-to-three-month figure quoted, so duration_days is unset and the juvenile scale is judgement.

vocalizations.trill.note: Description section: 'The song is a trill similar to the chipping sparrow's, except that the red-backed dark-eyed junco's song is more complex, similar to that of the yellow-eyed junco.' season_months is aligned to the April-July breeding period because the source dates song only implicitly.

vocalizations.chips.note: Description section: 'The call also resembles that of the black-throated blue warbler... Calls include tick sounds and very high-pitched tinkling chips.' It fills the shared program's alarm slot because the source describes no separate alarm call; loudness and cooldown are judgement.

look.note: Description section: 'Adult dark-eyed juncos generally have gray heads, necks, and breasts, gray or brown backs and wings, and a white belly, but show a confusing amount of variation in plumage details. The white outer tail feathers flash distinctively in flight... The bill is usually pale pinkish. Males tend to have darker, more conspicuous markings than females.' The palette carries the slate-grey hood and back with a white breast slot for the belly and the pale pink bill as the accent. The white outer tail feathers are not modelled: the tail is a single slot, so colouring it would make the whole tail white, which would be wrong; the flash is left to the species' own behaviour. Proportions are authored judgement.

behavior.note: Authored parameters for the shared perching-songbird program: food_tag is seed, three quarters of the year-round diet, used by the program for ground foraging; flee_m and wariness reflect a tame feeder bird that still flushes readily; nest_m1/nest_m2 span the April-July breeding period.
